title: Low-Level asyncio: Futures, Callbacks, Transports & Protocols
summary: Covers the machinery under async/await: Future objects, loop callbacks and thread-safe scheduling, the transport/protocol model behind create_connection and create_server, flow control, how StreamReader/StreamWriter sit on top of protocols, and asyncio subprocesses.

chapters.title: The Two Layers of asyncio
points: High-level API (asyncio.run, tasks, streams, create_subprocess_exec) is for application code; low-level API (loop methods, Futures, transports, protocols) is for library and framework authors
The event loop is a scheduler: it runs a ready queue of callbacks and polls a selector (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) for I/O readiness
One loop iteration (_run_once): compute timeout, poll selector, move due timers and I/O callbacks into the ready queue, run everything in it
A coroutine only runs when a Task wraps it; a Task is a Future subclass that steps the coroutine from a callback
await on a Future suspends the Task; the Future's completion schedules the Task's next step via call_soon
asyncio.get_running_loop() is the right way to get the loop inside a coroutine; get_event_loop() is deprecated there
SelectorEventLoop (Unix default) vs ProactorEventLoop (Windows default): readiness-based vs completion-based I/O
Layer diagram: coroutine → Task → Future → loop callbacks → transport → protocol → socket

chapters.title: Future Objects and loop.create_future
points: An asyncio.Future is a placeholder for a result not yet available; it has three states: pending, cancelled, finished
Create with loop.create_future(), not asyncio.Future() directly, so alternative loops (uvloop) can supply an optimised implementation
fut.set_result(v) and fut.set_exception(e) finish it; calling either twice raises InvalidStateError
fut.result() raises InvalidStateError if still pending, CancelledError if cancelled, or re-raises the stored exception
fut.cancel(msg=None) returns False if already done; fut.done() and fut.cancelled() report state
A Future is awaitable: __await__ yields the Future to the Task, which parks until the Future completes
Example: bridging a callback API with fut = loop.create_future(); api.start(on_done=fut.set_result); return await fut
Guard against late callbacks with 'if not fut.done(): fut.set_result(x)' when a timeout or cancel may have finished it first
asyncio.Future is not thread-safe and differs from concurrent.futures.Future; wrap_future() converts one to the other
An exception set on a Future nobody retrieves logs 'Future exception was never retrieved' when it is garbage-collected
Futures are bound to the loop that created them; awaiting one from another loop raises RuntimeError

chapters.title: Callbacks: add_done_callback and the Scheduling API
points: fut.add_done_callback(cb) calls cb(fut) once the Future completes; the callback receives the Future, not the result
Done callbacks never run inline: set_result schedules them with loop.call_soon, so they run on a later loop iteration
Adding a callback to an already-done Future still schedules it via call_soon rather than calling it immediately
Pass extra arguments with functools.partial, since add_done_callback accepts only the Future argument (plus context=)
fut.remove_done_callback(cb) removes every registration of cb and returns the count removed
loop.call_soon(cb, *args) appends to the ready queue and runs callbacks in FIFO order on the next iteration
loop.call_later(delay, cb) and loop.call_at(when, cb) use the loop's monotonic clock, loop.time()
call_soon returns a Handle and call_later/call_at return a TimerHandle; handle.cancel() prevents the run
Callbacks run inside a contextvars.Context copy (context= argument), so context variables propagate
An exception in a callback does not crash the loop: it goes to loop.call_exception_handler and gets logged
A slow callback blocks the entire loop; debug mode warns about callbacks slower than loop.slow_callback_duration (100 ms)

chapters.title: call_soon vs call_soon_threadsafe
points: loop.call_soon is not thread-safe: it only touches the ready queue and assumes the loop's own thread is calling
Calling call_soon from another thread can race on the queue, and a loop sleeping in select() will not wake up
loop.call_soon_threadsafe(cb) appends the callback and then writes a byte to the loop's self-pipe (_write_to_self) to wake the selector
Setting a Future from a worker thread: loop.call_soon_threadsafe(fut.set_result, value), never fut.set_result directly
asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop) submits a coroutine from another thread and returns a concurrent.futures.Future
loop.run_in_executor(None, fn) / asyncio.to_thread(fn) go the other way: blocking work runs in a thread and the loop gets back an awaitable Future
Debug mode (PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1) raises RuntimeError when a non-threadsafe loop method is called from the wrong thread
Signal handlers set with signal.signal must use call_soon_threadsafe too; loop.add_signal_handler handles this for you on Unix
Comparison table: call_soon (same thread, no wakeup, cheaper) vs call_soon_threadsafe (any thread, self-pipe wakeup)

chapters.title: Transports and Protocols: The Model
points: A transport owns the socket and does the I/O (how bytes move); a protocol holds your logic (what to do with the bytes)
Transports and protocols come in pairs: the loop builds the transport and calls protocol methods as events arrive
asyncio.Protocol callbacks: connection_made(transport), data_received(data), eof_received(), connection_lost(exc)
Callback order is guaranteed: connection_made → data_received* → eof_received? → connection_lost, and connection_lost is called exactly once
connection_lost(exc) receives None on a clean close or the exception on an error
If eof_received returns a truthy value the transport stays half-open; returning None/False closes it
data_received gets arbitrary chunks: one message can arrive split or several can arrive together, so the protocol must frame and buffer
Transport methods: write(data), writelines(), write_eof(), close(), abort(), get_extra_info('peername'/'socket'/'sslcontext')
Protocol methods are plain synchronous functions; you cannot await inside data_received, so spawn tasks with loop.create_task
BufferedProtocol (get_buffer/buffer_updated) receives into a preallocated buffer with no copy; DatagramProtocol and SubprocessProtocol cover other transport types

chapters.title: create_connection and create_server in Practice
points: transport, protocol = await loop.create_connection(lambda: MyProto(), host, port) opens a client connection
The first argument is a protocol factory (a callable), not an instance, because servers need a fresh protocol per connection
create_connection options: ssl=, server_hostname=, local_addr=, happy_eyeballs_delay= (RFC 8305), sock= for an existing socket
server = await loop.create_server(factory, host, port) returns an asyncio.Server listening on one or more sockets
Server lifecycle: async with server: await server.serve_forever(); server.close() plus await server.wait_closed() for shutdown
create_server options: reuse_address, reuse_port, backlog (default 100), start_serving=False to delay accepting
Echo server example: connection_made stores the transport; data_received calls self.transport.write(data)
Getting a result out of a protocol: pass a Future into the factory (lambda: Proto(on_done=fut)) and set it in connection_lost
Also available: loop.create_unix_connection/create_unix_server for Unix sockets and create_datagram_endpoint for UDP
Comparison: raw protocols are fastest with the least overhead, but you must handle framing, backpressure and shutdown yourself

chapters.title: Flow Control: Backpressure Both Ways
points: transport.write() never blocks: bytes the socket cannot send yet are queued in the transport's write buffer
Write buffer limits: the high-water mark (default 64 KiB) and low-water mark (default high/4) are set with transport.set_write_buffer_limits(high, low)
When the buffer rises above high the transport calls protocol.pause_writing(); once it drains below low it calls resume_writing()
The protocol must actually stop producing on pause_writing; if it ignores it, write() keeps buffering until memory runs out
get_write_buffer_size() and get_write_buffer_limits() let you inspect the buffer state
Read side: transport.pause_reading() stops calling data_received (the socket is removed from the selector); resume_reading() restarts it
Pausing reads fills the kernel receive buffer, which shrinks the TCP window and slows the remote sender (real backpressure)
transport.is_reading() reports read state; since 3.7, pausing or resuming twice is a no-op, not an error
Pattern: count queued work, call pause_reading above a limit and resume_reading below a lower one (hysteresis avoids flapping)
Diagram: fast producer → write buffer → high mark → pause_writing → drain → low mark → resume_writing

chapters.title: How Streams Are Built on Protocols
points: asyncio.open_connection() calls loop.create_connection with a StreamReaderProtocol and returns (StreamReader, StreamWriter)
asyncio.start_server(client_cb, host, port) wraps create_server; each connection calls client_cb(reader, writer), and a coroutine client_cb runs as a Task
StreamReaderProtocol.data_received calls reader.feed_data(data); eof_received calls reader.feed_eof()
StreamReader keeps an internal bytearray buffer; read(n), readline(), readexactly(n) and readuntil(sep) await a waiter Future until enough data arrives
Read backpressure: when the reader's buffer exceeds 2 × limit (default limit 64 KiB) it calls transport.pause_reading(), and resumes once consumers drain it
StreamWriter.write() is a thin wrapper over transport.write(); await writer.drain() blocks while the protocol is paused (FlowControlMixin)
drain() awaits a Future that resume_writing completes, which turns pause_writing callbacks into await-style backpressure
readline() raises ValueError/LimitOverrunError when a line exceeds the limit; readexactly raises IncompleteReadError on early EOF
Close correctly: writer.close(), then await writer.wait_closed()
Comparison: streams give coroutine ergonomics and built-in backpressure; protocols avoid per-read Futures and are faster under heavy load

chapters.title: Subprocesses with create_subprocess_exec
points: proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec('ls', '-l', stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE) passes program and args separately, with no shell
create_subprocess_shell(cmd) goes through /bin/sh; any untrusted input needs shlex.quote or it becomes a shell-injection risk
Under the hood: loop.subprocess_exec(protocol_factory, ...) plus a SubprocessStreamProtocol that exposes proc.stdin/stdout/stderr as streams
The Process object provides pid, returncode (None while running), await proc.wait(), send_signal(), terminate(), kill()
stdout, stderr = await proc.communicate(input=b'...') writes stdin, reads both pipes to EOF, and waits for exit
Deadlock: await proc.wait() with PIPE output can hang once the OS pipe buffer (~64 KiB) fills; use communicate() or read the pipes concurrently
Stream line by line: async for line in proc.stdout, for live output from long-running commands
Add a timeout with asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), 10); on TimeoutError, proc.kill() and then await proc.wait() to reap the child
stderr=asyncio.subprocess.STDOUT merges the two streams; DEVNULL discards output
Windows needs ProactorEventLoop (the default since 3.8) for subprocesses; on Unix a child watcher / pidfd reaps exited children

chapters.title: Low-Level asyncio Cheatsheet
points: Future: loop.create_future() → set_result/set_exception → await fut; guard with 'if not fut.done()'
Callbacks: add_done_callback(cb) passes the Future; use functools.partial for extra args; callbacks are always scheduled with call_soon
Scheduling: call_soon (same thread) | call_soon_threadsafe (other thread, wakes the loop) | call_later/call_at (timers)
Cross-thread: run_coroutine_threadsafe (thread → loop) | to_thread / run_in_executor (loop → thread)
Protocol order: connection_made → data_received* → eof_received → connection_lost (exactly once)
Client/server: create_connection(factory, host, port) | create_server(factory, host, port) → serve_forever
Write backpressure: set_write_buffer_limits → pause_writing/resume_writing; in streams: await writer.drain()
Read backpressure: transport.pause_reading()/resume_reading(); StreamReader pauses automatically above 2 × limit
Streams = StreamReaderProtocol + StreamReader.feed_data + StreamWriter over the transport
Subprocess: create_subprocess_exec + communicate(); never wait() while PIPE output is unread
Top mistakes: no awaiting inside data_received, no Future calls from threads, never assume data_received gets whole messages
Pick streams by default; drop to protocols for maximum throughput or custom framing
